teaser: A toddler falls over in a Venetian square, and a whole morning stops around him.
review_notes:
Date c. 1725 is the usual one; some scholars place it slightly later.
The yard as a temporary site for rebuilding the church of San Vidal: National Gallery account.
Campanile of Santa Maria della Carità collapsed in 1744.
The child urinating in fright is described by the National Gallery but cannot be made out in our image.
The bird in the lower-left window is read as a cock (National Gallery); it is tiny in our image.
Likely painted for a Venetian patron rather than a tourist: an inference, flagged as such in the text.
Beaumont gift: promised 1823, entered the National Gallery 1828.

lesson.text: A small child has just tipped over backward onto the dirt. His mother lunges toward him, arms flung wide. Another child stands and stares. Above them, a woman leans out of a window to see what the noise is about. One second of one morning in Venice, around 1725, and Canaletto stopped the clock on it.
The fall happens in a corner of this big view. Can you find the child on the ground?

spots.title: The tumble
spots.text: He lies on his back with his legs in the air. His mother rushes in from the left. Close study of the real canvas shows he is wetting himself in fright.

lesson.text: It is an odd corner of Venice to choose. No palace front, no festival, no famous square. This is Campo San Vidal seen from behind, at a moment when it was cluttered with blocks of stone. Masons were using the open ground as a workshop, most likely for repairs to the nearby church of San Vidal.
Canaletto never called it “The Stonemason's Yard.” The nickname was added later. The yard was temporary, and the square has been a plain open space again for centuries.

Everything in the view agrees about the time of day. Sunlight comes in low from the left and throws long shadows across the ground. The city is waking up, and each household is busy with its first chores.

lesson.title: Early chores
lesson.text: Four people, or creatures, starting their day.

spots.title: The neighbor
spots.text: A woman leans far out over a sill where bedding is airing. She is the first witness of the fall down below.

spots.title: A bird at the window
spots.text: In the dark opening just below, look for a red and white bird. It is read as a cock, the usual signal of daybreak.

spots.title: The spinner
spots.text: On a wooden balcony across the yard, a woman draws out thread with a hand spindle, working in the first good light.

spots.title: The mason
spots.text: A man bends over a large hollowed block and works its rim. The pale stone came by boat from across the Adriatic.

lesson.text: Canaletto was about twenty-eight. His real name was Giovanni Antonio Canal, and “Canaletto” just means “little Canal”: his father Bernardo painted scenery for the opera houses of Venice, and the son started out beside him. He left the theater a few years before this picture. The training stayed.
The view is laid out like the stage of a theater.

lines.label: Left wing
lines.text: A slice of pink house closes the scene on this side, like a painted flat sliding in from the wings.

lines.label: Right wing
lines.text: The taller house does the same on the other side. Its roof slants down toward the middle and steers your eye inward.

lines.label: The backdrop
lines.text: Across the Grand Canal, the far bank runs flat like a painted backcloth: church, bell tower, rooftops.

lines.label: The tower
lines.text: One tall vertical pins the composition, placed well off center so the sky has room to open on the right.

lesson.text: A convincing view is still a designed one: wings at the sides, action up front, a backdrop behind.

The paint is unlike the bright, crisp Venice he became famous for. It is laid on thick and loose over a dark ground, with a heavy sky and deep brown shadows. The size is generous, about 124 by 163 centimeters (49 by 64 inches). The humble subject suggests a local buyer who knew the spot, though no document says who.
The bell tower across the water is gone. It collapsed in 1744, less than twenty years after Canaletto painted it, and was never rebuilt.

Stand here today and you would be at the foot of the Accademia Bridge, which did not exist yet: people crossed by gondola ferry. The church opposite, Santa Maria della Carità, is no longer a church. It is part of the Accademia Galleries, Venice's great museum of painting.

spots.title: The Carità
spots.text: The long brick flank of the church with its tall windows. Today its interior holds museum rooms.

spots.title: The lost bell tower
spots.text: Slim, with a cone-shaped spire. This painting is one of the best records of how it looked.

spots.title: Gondolas
spots.text: Black boats with small cabins wait on the green water of the Grand Canal. One boatman stands upright among them.

spots.title: A Venetian chimney
spots.text: Wide and flared like an upside-down bell. The shape was meant to catch sparks, in a city terrified of fire.

spots.title: The shed
spots.text: A rough plank lean-to shelters the masons. Canaletto paints every warped board and its shadow.

spots.title: Washing
spots.text: White linen hangs from the upper shutters and catches the sun, the brightest notes in the picture.

lesson.text: The English collector Sir George Beaumont owned this canvas. In 1823 he promised his pictures to the nation to push the government into founding a National Gallery, and this one arrived there in 1828.

Canaletto painted few scenes like it afterward. Sunny views of the famous sights sold faster. So this painting leaves a question hanging: what would he have become if he had kept looking at the back yards of his city, and at the toddlers falling over in them?

quiz.question: What small accident is happening in the foreground?
options: A block of stone has cracked
quiz.explanation: A toddler lies on his back while his mother rushes toward him.

quiz.question: What did Canaletto's father do for a living?
options: He painted scenery for the theater
quiz.explanation: Bernardo Canal painted opera sets, and his son trained with him.

quiz.question: What happened to the bell tower seen across the canal?
options: It was moved to another island
quiz.explanation: It fell down in 1744 and was not rebuilt.

quiz.question: What is the church of Santa Maria della Carità today?
quiz.explanation: The building now belongs to Venice's main museum of painting.

quiz.question: How does the paint handling differ from Canaletto's later views?
options: It is thicker, looser and darker
It is done entirely in watercolor
It uses only black and white
quiz.explanation: He worked loosely over a dark ground, unlike his later bright, crisp style.

facts.explanation: His family name was Canal and his father Bernardo was also a painter.

facts.text: The Accademia Bridge is visible on the left of the painting.
facts.explanation: The bridge did not exist yet; people crossed by gondola ferry.

facts.text: The title “The Stonemason's Yard” was chosen by Canaletto himself.
facts.explanation: It is a later nickname for a view of Campo San Vidal.
